draft.title: How interest rates affect spending
card: When the RBA raises the cash rate, banks tend to raise their rates too. Borrowing becomes dearer, because loans such as home loans cost more in interest.
Saving also becomes more rewarding, because savers earn more interest on their deposits. Some people choose to save more and spend less.
With less spending, demand for goods and services grows more slowly. Businesses find it harder to raise prices, so inflation slows.
Cutting the cash rate does the opposite. Borrowing is cheaper and saving earns less, so spending tends to rise, and so can inflation.
draft.remember: A higher cash rate tends to slow spending and inflation. A lower rate tends to lift them.

a.q: The RBA raises the cash rate and banks raise their loan rates. What is the likely effect on household spending?
opts: It tends to slow, as borrowing costs more
It tends to rise, as saving earns more
It tends to rise, as borrowing costs more
It tends to slow, as saving earns less
a.why: Higher loan rates make borrowing dearer, and higher savings rates make saving more rewarding, so households tend to spend less. The tempting option says saving earns less, but a higher cash rate tends to lift savings rates.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the cost of a loan.

b.q: Inflation in Australia is rising quickly because people are spending a lot. Which RBA move would most likely slow it, and why?
opts: Raise the cash rate, so spending slows
Cut the cash rate, so spending slows
Raise the cash rate, so borrowing is cheaper
Cut the cash rate, so saving is more rewarding
b.why: Raising the cash rate makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so spending slows and inflation eases. Cutting the rate does the opposite and would tend to push spending up, not slow it.
b.clue: To slow spending, should borrowing be cheaper or dearer?

a.best: It tends to slow, as borrowing costs more

b.best: Raise the cash rate, so spending slows
